title: After-hours stitchwork: conference + paper harvest (context economics)
content:
Late-night synthesis notes from a chaotic week: conference panels + a few papers skimmed on the train. Rapid-fire, chopped, and half-formed — keeping a record before this migrates into a ticket or a PR.

What I read / attended:
- Panel: "Operational tactics for long-context models" (small workshop, awkward mic, surprisingly pragmatic). Key line: "treat KV cache as storage tier, not ephemeral RAM".
- Paper: "Adaptive Eviction for KV Caches in Transformer Inference" (arXiv 2406.12345) — proposes a tiny RL agent to decide evictions based on future-token heuristics.
- Paper: "Sparse Attention + Chunked KV for 100k windows" (arXiv 2305.16290) — good ablations on chunk size vs cross-chunk attention cost.
- Blog: notes from Dasha/ByteScale talk (panel) about graceful degradation using variant models (quantized fallback).

Top-line takeaways (TL;DR):
- Eviction heuristics matter more than cache size once you hit >4k seqs. Simple recency + access frequency gets you ~70%, but where you lose is the tail (rare but high-value prefixes).
- Treating KV cache like a tiered store (hot / warm / cold) aligns well with Redwood Dedicated burst behavior: hot stays on GPU local, warm could be prefetched from nearby node, cold evicted and reconstructed on demand.
- Quantized fallbacks are effectively a latency/cost envelope: use low-bit variant for non-critical completions and warm/hot for top-k beams.

Questions and friction points (brain dump):
- How quickly can we snapshot KV state for canary rollouts? If a user pins a model but we switch runtime variant, do we lose alignment?
- Does stochastic eviction amplify hallucination risk for retrieval-augmented flows? If the relevant doc gets evicted mid-session, downstream RAG logic needs robust fallback.
- Ops complexity: tiered cache implies data movement — need bandwidth accounting in Redwood Console (per-route).

Experimental ideas (prioritized):
1) Micro-probe: implement a small LRU+LFU hybrid with tunable decay for a single model on staging. Measure token-level hit-rate vs latency under synthetic session traces (use existing sim traces: INF-eviction-sim-2026). TODO: turn this into a spike PR: repo kv-cache-protos, branch 'stitch-probe-aya'.
2) Cold-prefetch policy: when context hits a recognized retrieval anchor (e.g., RAG doc id seen in prompt), prefetch cached fragments into warm tier. Test regression on RAG-heavy workloads.
3) Quantized-fallback experiment: send 5% of requests to 4-bit variant + adjust tracing to capture semantic drift metrics in console. Hook up lightweight evals to detect regression (prompt set: evals/kv-fallback-anchors).

Notes to self / crude plan for a short write-up to send to Kenji: 
- 1 page: problem statement (tail misses + cost), 2 pages: existing literature (include the two papers + panel notes), 1 page: proposed spike experiments + measurement matrix, 1 page: expected failure modes and rollback plan.
- Slack thread: ping SRE and runtime to check feasibility of warm-tier placement (Kenji / Nora).

Ops + Redwood-specific implications:
- Billing: warm-tier traffic should be surfaced in Redwood Console (per-route token delta + network egress). If we prefetch aggressively, cost model changes. Need a quick mockup for Product (console-and-rollouts).
- Rollouts: snapshotting KV across model variants is tricky. Consider a conservative approach: only allow variant switch at session boundary unless we have a compatibility shim.
- Observability: need a new trace tag 'kv-tier' (values: hot|warm|cold|miss) and expose histograms for time-to-prefetch. This is small but high-impact for debugging customer regressions.

Links worth saving (raw):
- Adaptive eviction paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12345
- Sparse attention chunking: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16290
- Internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-protos/pull/42
- Jira spike: INF-2481

Action items (short):
- [ ] Create spike branch and add simple LRU+decay eviction implementation (owner: me) — target: 2 days.
- [ ] Draft 1-page problem brief for Kenji & Nora — target: EOD Friday.
- [ ] Add 'kv-tier' tag to tracing schema proposal doc and drop on SRE's lane.
- [ ] Run warm-prefetch sim with 10k synthetic sessions and capture hit-rate vs overhead.

Personal reflections (why I care):
- This feels like high-leverage: a small change in eviction/prefetch could drop per-token costs for long-session customers significantly, and reduce tail-latency spikes that burn developer trust. Also, less heroic infra work (no massive sharding) — more policy/heuristic improvements.
- I'm worried about complexity creep: tiered caches often become leaky abstractions. Keep the API simple: we expose 'preferred_ttl' and runtime optimizes placement.

Misc scribbles / heuristics to test:
- Prefetch only when retrieval score > 0.7 OR doc recency within session < 5 turns.
- If an anchor doc is evicted and reconstructed, penalize future prefetch probability by small factor to avoid oscillation.
- Track "semantic hit" not just token hit: use embedding similarity to check whether evicted fragment would have materially changed logits for next 16 tokens. Bad idea to do at runtime, but useful offline evaluation metric.

Final: rough timeline idea — spike (2w) -> small A/B (4w) -> product decision. Share this with Kenji tomorrow and see if we can get a tiny allocation on dedicated staging cluster for the probe.

Notes to export into a nicer doc later: paste the key bullets into a 1-pager, include a micro-graph of hit-rate vs seq-length (I have sim results locally), and propose two simple KPIs: session hit-rate and tail-latency-95.

-- aya
